rows.claim: Supplier renegotiations targeting 80-120bps COGS improvement are board-approved for Q1 FY25 but lack contracted terms or documented supplier commitment, representing a load-bearing assumption for Food and Home margin recovery.
rows.evidence:
- Group COGS rate moved from 61.8% (FY22) to 63.6% (FY24), a
  180bps deterioration driven by Food (220bps) and Home
  (280bps). Premium and Online held rate within ±30bps.
- Group opex rate held at 25.7% (FY22) → 25.8% (FY24); the
  apparent stability masks a 90bps rise in marketing offset by
  a 120bps fall in store payroll (post-rationalisation).
- Working capital cycle: 38 days (FY22) → 51 days (FY24). Food
  and Home together explain 12 of the 13 day deterioration —
  inventory builds in both, partly cyclical, partly the
  symptom of slowing turn.
## Implementation constraints
- The board has signed off on supplier-side renegotiations Q1 FY25
  but has explicitly excluded SKU rationalisation from the H1 plan
  on customer-experience concerns.
- Marketing budget is fixed at FY24 levels (£8.4m) for FY25;
  no additional pricing-test budget approved.
- The sponsor's exit window (24 months) caps the realistic payback
  horizon at 18 months — actions requiring 24m+ payback are out
  of scope.
- Albright operates a single ERP (SAP S/4HANA, deployed FY22) so
  segment-level price changes are technically feasible within a
  3-week change cycle.

rows.evidence:

  "in-store experience" above price as decision drivers in 64%
  of category responses.
- **Food shoppers** show elasticity of -1.6 on staples and -0.9
  on private label — staple-pricing increases trigger immediate
  basket-mix shifts to discounters; private-label increases are
  better absorbed.
- **Home customers** show elasticity of -2.1 on big-ticket items
  (>£40 ASP) and -1.4 on the long tail. The high big-ticket
  elasticity confirms the LFL data: Home is structurally
  price-sensitive at the SKU level Albright competes on.
- **Online customers** show the lowest blended elasticity (-0.6)
  but the highest trial-rate response (+18% trial uplift on
  promotional pricing) — the channel's pricing power is
  promotional rather than structural.

# Retail Sector Primer (UK + US, Boutique View)
This primer codifies the firm's working view of the consumer-retail
sector across the UK and US — the structural shape, the players we
actually track, the KPIs that matter on diligence, and the trends we
expect partners to refer to in client meetings without re-reading the
trade press. It is fully synthetic and produced for fixture use only;
no real client data is reproduced.
## Market structure
The retail market in both the UK and the US is bifurcating along
roughly the same axis: scaled omnichannel operators on one side and
specialist single-channel operators on the other, with the squeezed
middle (regional chains, mid-market department stores, second-tier
grocers) shedding share each year.
In the UK the three structural realities a partner should be able to
state in any client conversation are:

rows.claim: The discounter pair (Aldi and Lidl) has taken roughly 18% combined share in UK grocery over the last decade, establishing aggressive pricing as the competitive baseline for value segments. Any grocery-exposed segment must price relative to this benchmark or differentiate clearly. FALSIFIABLE IF: This business's segments are non-grocery (DIY, fashion, specialty) where discounter dynamics do not apply, rendering grocery pricing benchmarks irrelevant.
rows.evidence:
1. The grocery sector is a five-player game (Tesco, Sainsbury's, Asda,
   Morrisons, plus the discounter pair Aldi and Lidl) and the
   discounter pair has taken roughly 18% combined share over the last
   decade. Anything below that top tier — Iceland, Co-op, Waitrose,
   Ocado-as-pureplay — competes on a clearly differentiated proposition
   or it doesn't survive the next cycle.
2. High-street non-food retail has been hollowed out. The viable
   non-grocery formats today are out-of-town value (B&M, Home Bargains,
   The Range), branded specialty (JD Sports, Greggs, Pret), and the
   premium-experiential end (Selfridges, Liberty, John Lewis as a
   wounded but persistent format). Mid-market high-street fashion
   below £40 ASP has effectively migrated online or bankrupt.
3. The DIY / homewares segment is structurally smaller than its US
   equivalent and dominated by Kingfisher (B&Q + Screwfix) and Wickes,
   with the Travis Perkins B2B route distinct from consumer-facing
   sheds.

rows.claim: The UK retail market is bifurcating between scaled omnichannel operators and specialist single-channel operators, with the squeezed middle (regional chains, mid-market department stores, second-tier grocers) shedding share each year. This structural pattern determines viable pricing architectures: omnichannel players optimize cost-to-serve, specialists compete on differentiation, and mid-market players face structural disadvantage. rows.claim: Decision criteria for entry mode selection include strategic and financial filters: geography, size, ownership, integration risk, gross margin thresholds, revenue growth rates, and customer concentration, ensuring the financial profile supports deal mechanics without excessive assumptions.
rows.evidence:
The first cut on candidates filters by the four hard constraints
before any deeper analysis. A miss on any one knocks the candidate
out of the screen entirely.
1. **Geography.** UK and Western Europe primary, with case-by-case
   inclusion of Nordic and DACH. We avoid US-only targets unless the
   buyer has an existing US tax structure and US-side legal counsel
   already engaged.
2. **Size band.** EV in the £100m–£500m corridor; revenue typically
   £40m–£250m; EBITDA £15m–£80m. Below £15m EBITDA the deal economics
   rarely support the diligence cost. Above £80m EBITDA the auction
   dynamics are different and screening adds less value.
3. **Ownership.** Founder-owned or PE-backed (single-sponsor); we
   exclude family-trust holdings unless succession is the explicit
   trigger. Listed targets fall outside this playbook — different
   rules apply (see the public-markets playbook).
4. **Sector momentum.** The target operates in a sector with clear
   unit economics, growing or stable demand, and an identifiable
   value-creation lever the buyer can execute against.
Candidates that survive the first cut go through the second-pass
financial filter below.

rows.claim: Pilot-first entry strategies reduce commitment risk: sequenced single-market entry at constrained headcount (per evidence on 47 expansions) outperforms parallel approaches, and two-quarter validation programs can inform full-scale entry decisions, though the 80%+ accuracy claim from internal patterns requires independent verification and may not generalize to Germany/France B2B SaaS specifically.
rows.evidence: At 12-headcount caps, sequenced entry to a single anchor market produced 2.3x the qualified pipeline in 18 months vs split parallel entries (n=47 expansions).

rows.claim: Net revenue retention in German Mittelstand B2B SaaS averages 117% versus 109% in French mid-market, indicating slower initial sales but materially higher long-term account value and expansion potential.
rows.evidence: Net revenue retention in German Mittelstand B2B SaaS averages 117% vs 109% in French mid-market — slow to land but stickier.

rows.claim: At 12-headcount scale, sequenced single-market entry produced 2.3x the qualified pipeline in 18 months compared to parallel split entries across 47 observed expansions, indicating focus is critical at this team size.

rows.evidence: Fully-loaded cost for a 6-person early-stage GTM team is approximately €1.05M/yr in Paris vs €1.32M/yr in Munich at comparable seniority.

rows.claim: France's UGAP SaaS Public Cloud framework streamlined €340M in public-sector SaaS purchases in 2024, offering an accelerated procurement path unavailable in Germany for vendors who qualify.
rows.evidence: UGAP and the SaaS Public Cloud framework streamline public-sector SaaS purchases, with €340M flowing through the framework in 2024.

rows.claim: German enterprise buyers require in-country data residency in 68% of RFPs versus 41% in France, adding infrastructure complexity and unquantified cost even where GDPR does not mandate it.
rows.evidence: German enterprise buyers more frequently require in-country data residency (68% of RFPs vs 41% in France), even where GDPR alone does not mandate it.

rows.evidence: Average B2B SaaS procurement cycle in German Mittelstand: 7.2 months, vs 4.8 months in France for comparable deal sizes.

rows.evidence: France posted 22% YoY growth in B2B SaaS spend in 2024, outpacing Germany's 14% — driven by public-sector digitization mandates.

rows.claim: Germany's B2B SaaS market reached approximately €18.4B in 2024, making it the largest in continental Europe and roughly 1.6x the size of France's market.

This pattern suggests pilots can de-risk full-scale commitments, but the pilot must have explicit success criteria: €150K qualified pipeline, 15% trial-to-paid conversion, and validation of 7.2-month procurement cycle by month 6.

rows.claim: Industrial Cleaning segment (24% of revenue) decelerated sharply from 6.0% growth in FY22 to 2.0% in FY24, generating £43.2m revenue and £4.8m EBITDA (11.1% margin), pressured by cyclical industrial customer cost constraints and two new regional competitors in the Midlands.
rows.evidence:
### 2.2 Industrial Cleaning (24% of revenue)
Manufacturing, food-production, and pharmaceutical-grade industrial
cleaning. FY24 revenue £43.2m, EBITDA £4.8m (11.1% margin), +2.0%
YoY. Largely transactional revenue (52% one-off jobs, 48% rolling
quarterly contracts). Pharmaceutical-grade cleaning carries the
highest margin (~17%) but is a smaller share of the segment;
manufacturing-grade is competitive and price-led.
The segment's growth has decelerated from 6.0% in FY22 to 2.0% in
FY24 — partly cyclical (industrial customers under cost pressure),
partly competitive (two new regional players in the Midlands).
### 2.3 Mechanical Services (16% of revenue)
Project-based mechanical engineering: chiller installation,
pressurised systems, ventilation refurbishment. FY24 revenue £28.8m,
EBITDA £5.2m (18.1% margin), +6.0% YoY. The highest-margin segment
on a project basis but lumpy: 65% of the segment's annual revenue
typically lands in two pricing windows (May/June, October/November)
tied to customer capex cycles.

rows.claim: Understanding the customer profile requires identifying who the business serves best and why they choose the business, validated through customer interviews, win-loss analysis, and competitive teardown rather than demographic labels.

1. **Who is the customer the business serves best, and why?**
   Cohort-level revenue concentration, NPS by segment, product
   penetration by segment. The answer must be a description, not a
   demographic — "logistics director at a 200-person 3PL" beats
   "35-55 year old male decision maker".
2. **What is the single biggest reason the customer chooses us?**
   This must be testable: customer interviews, win-loss analysis,
   competitive teardown. If three different team members answer
   this question three different ways, the engagement isn't ready
   to move past week 1.
3. **What is the unit-economic shape of the business today?**
   Contribution margin per customer per year, payback period on
   acquisition, lifetime value, retention curve. Growth strategy
   built on shaky unit economics produces growth that is value-
   destructive.
4. **What is the addressable market the business actually competes
   in, sized bottom-up?** Top-down market sizing is a sanity check
   on the bottom-up number; the bottom-up sizing is the analytic
   primary.
5. **What capacity does the business have to absorb growth?**
   Operational, financial, talent. Growth that exceeds absorbable
   capacity produces system failures (stockouts, NPS collapse, key
   person attrition) that wipe out the financial gain.
6. **What does the next-12-months counterfactual look like with no
   intervention?** This is the baseline against which the growth
   strategy will be judged.

# Retail Sector Primer (UK + US, Boutique View)
This primer codifies the firm's working view of the consumer-retail
sector across the UK and US — the structural shape, the players we
actually track, the KPIs that matter on diligence, and the trends we
expect partners to refer to in client meetings without re-reading the
trade press. It is fully synthetic and produced for fixture use only;
no real client data is reproduced.
## Market structure
The retail market in both the UK and the US is bifurcating along
roughly the same axis: scaled omnichannel operators on one side and
specialist single-channel operators on the other, with the squeezed
middle (regional chains, mid-market department stores, second-tier
grocers) shedding share each year.

## What we ask buyers to commit to before the engagement
For a sector-screen or growth-strategy mandate in retail the firm
expects the buyer to articulate:
- The strategic rationale in one sentence (consolidation? geographic
  fill? channel acquisition? data asset acquisition?).
- The exit horizon and the named comparable buyer set.
- The acceptable level of post-close transformation — heavy turnaround
  cases require a different team than bolt-on consolidation.
- A clear position on physical estate: shrink, hold, or grow the
  store base. A buyer who is undecided on this dimension will not
  be able to act on the screen output.
These conditions are non-negotiable for retail engagements; without
them the work spirals into a "broad market scan" that is not what
the firm is paid to deliver.

rows.claim: The US grocery sector is regional with no national-scale grocer comparable to Tesco in the UK; Walmart and Costco approximate national footprint but operate hybrid format models, while Kroger plus Albertsons covers the heartland, making regional strength more important than national share for any acquisition thesis.
rows.evidence:
1. Grocery is regional. There is no national-scale grocer in the US in
   the way Tesco is national in the UK. Walmart and Costco approximate
   a national footprint but operate hybrid format models, Kroger plus
   Albertsons (post-merger or not) covers the heartland, and regional
   strength matters more than national share for any acquisition
   thesis.
2. The mall channel is still the relevant unit of analysis for
   apparel-and-accessories diligence: A-class malls are stable to
   growing, B-class are flat to declining, C and D class are in
   secular decline. Tenant mix and anchor health matter more than
   the headline footfall figure.
3. The off-price channel (TJX, Ross Stores, Burlington) absorbs a
   meaningful share of inventory liquidity from full-price retail and
   a healthy off-price relationship is a feature of a target's brand
   ecosystem, not a sell signal.
## KPIs on diligence
The five KPIs the firm consistently re-derives from raw data on a
retail target:

rows.claim: Customer cohort retention—at minimum 12-month repeat purchase rate by acquisition cohort—is essential. Retail brands frequently show flat or growing top-line while underlying cohort retention is collapsing; cohort decomposition is the only way to detect this terminal pattern.
rows.evidence:
- **Like-for-like (LFL) sales growth** decomposed into traffic, basket
  size, and price/mix. A LFL number presented in isolation is half
  evidence; insist on the decomposition before forming a view.
- **Gross margin walk** showing rate vs cost-of-goods inflation and
  promo intensity. A flat gross margin in an inflationary year is
  often a worse sign than a 50bp drop, because it implies promo cuts
  are masking input cost pressure.
- **Stock turn** measured by category rather than blended. Category
  weighted-average stock turn buries the long-tail SKUs where
  obsolescence write-downs hide.
- **Customer cohort retention** — at minimum 12-month repeat purchase
  rate by acquisition cohort, not blended. Retail brands frequently
  show flat or growing top-line while underlying cohort retention is
  collapsing; cohort decomposition is the only way to see it.
- **Store-level four-wall EBITDA** with a per-store distribution
  rather than a chain mean. The mean hides the bottom-decile stores
  whose closure economics dominate the post-close case.

rows.claim: Discounters Aldi and Lidl have captured approximately 18% combined market share in UK grocery over the past decade, forcing retailers below the top five (Tesco, Sainsbury's, Asda, Morrisons, plus the discounter pair) to compete on clearly differentiated propositions or face exit in the next cycle.
rows.evidence:
1. The grocery sector is a five-player game (Tesco, Sainsbury's, Asda,
   Morrisons, plus the discounter pair Aldi and Lidl) and the
   discounter pair has taken roughly 18% combined share over the last
   decade. Anything below that top tier — Iceland, Co-op, Waitrose,
   Ocado-as-pureplay — competes on a clearly differentiated proposition
   or it doesn't survive the next cycle.
2. High-street non-food retail has been hollowed out. The viable
   non-grocery formats today are out-of-town value (B&M, Home Bargains,
   The Range), branded specialty (JD Sports, Greggs, Pret), and the
   premium-experiential end (Selfridges, Liberty, John Lewis as a
   wounded but persistent format). Mid-market high-street fashion
   below £40 ASP has effectively migrated online or bankrupt.
3. The DIY / homewares segment is structurally smaller than its US
   equivalent and dominated by Kingfisher (B&Q + Screwfix) and Wickes,
   with the Travis Perkins B2B route distinct from consumer-facing
   sheds.
